root.name: Lion Defense: Bayonet Attack
root.moves: 1. e4 d6 2. d4 Nf6 3. Nc3 Nbd7 4. g4

overview: White plays 4.g4 against the Lion set-up with ...Nbd7, grabbing space on the kingside and threatening g5 to kick the f6 knight. Black normally replies ...e5 or ...c5 and aims to undermine the centre, often with ...h6 to blunt the g-pawn. Both sides castle in different places and the game becomes a race.

white_ideas.idea: Push g5 and h4 to cramp the kingside
Support with Be3, Qd2 and a possible long castle

black_ideas.idea: Use ...h6 and ...Nb6 to meet the pawn advance

typical_structures.structure: Tense e4/d4 centre against ...d6 with open flanks
Kingside pawn storm against a Black king that may castle either side

character.notes: Pawns are thrown forward and both kings can come under fire, so a slip loses quickly.

gambit.notes: No material has been given; the g-pawn is protected.

soundness.notes: Black is sound and the g4 advance weakens White, so both sides are playable.

structure.notes: The centre stays in tension while pawns are advanced on the wing.

approach.notes: An established way of meeting the Lion and the Pirc, if less common than 4.f4 or 4.Be3.

level.notes: Plans and timing matter more than memorised lines.

sublines_that_differ.name: Quiet 4.Nf3
sublines_that_differ.moves: 1. e4 d6 2. d4 Nf6 3. Nc3 Nbd7 4. Nf3

character.reason: The g-pawn lunge makes both sides take risks on opposite wings.

soundness.reason: Neither side is considered losing by force.

structure.reason: The centre is under tension rather than locked or opened.

approach.reason: It is a recognised main-line branch against the Lion and Pirc.

level.reason: The plans are clear enough but the timing needs experience.

plans.reason: White pushes the g- and h-pawns to cramp and attack.
